source.title: Scaling and Data Saturation in Protein Language Models
source.authors: Aviv Spinner; Erika Debenedictis; Corey M. Hudson

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how downstream protein-function prediction changes with pretraining-data growth and reports nonmonotonic results, qualifying the expectation of predictable scaling in this setting.
record.gate_note: The study measures downstream protein-fitness prediction, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy, parameter-count or compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocations. Its numerical result for best-year average performance and its other reported downstream outcomes are included only where they bear on data scaling or downstream predictability. Cited scaling-law results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies the downstream-scaling question to a new setting: protein language models. It tracks protein-fitness prediction across 14 AMPLIFY models pretrained on growing yearly UniRef100 snapshots. Its results bear on V6 (downstream performance improving predictably with data scale). It measures no pretraining loss, power-law fit, parameter or compute sweep, or allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with two additions. The authors stress that they find no evidence of data saturation: performance improves, but not monotonically, with added data, and the trend differs between unsupervised and supervised experiments. They also say unsupervised β-Lactamase predictions do not yet consistently beat the supervised baseline.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares protein-fitness prediction across time-based pretraining-data snapshots, using Spearman correlation on ProteinGym assays. It does not sweep parameters, tokens, or compute to fit held-out-loss power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported trends differ by MSA depth, assay type, evaluation split, and whether prediction is unsupervised or uses labeled experimental datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: In the β-Lactamase cross-dataset transfer, ridge-regression performance improves monotonically as experimental labeled datasets are added. Two- and three-dataset models beat all zero-shot baselines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream protein-fitness prediction scales more reliably with labeled experimental data than with unlabeled pretraining-data growth.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The study examines one suite of AMPLIFY checkpoints and notes that the models have relatively small parameter counts and single-seed training. Many trends are presented in figures without per-condition numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The outcomes are downstream protein-fitness correlations, not held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No power-law form of loss is measured for protein models. Downstream supervised (ridge) results do not test the power-law form for fine-tuning or transfer.

Scaling in parameters or compute (single 120M size) is not tested. The relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss is not measured. Only pretraining-data snapshot size varies, with tokens and compute per model unstated.
No fitted exponents or comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Random-split supervised results by MSA depth: low-MSA proteins perform better with models trained on earlier UniRef100 snapshots (a reversal); medium and high MSA show a smaller range.
Best-year average zero-shot Spearman of 0.38 across ProteinGym. This is the only absolute level reported for the snapshot sweep.

record.verdict_notes: All models are a single size (AMPLIFY 120M), single-seed. The 'scale' axis is yearly UniRef100 snapshot size, which also changes data composition and redundancy (the UniRef50/100 ratio declines). The text does not say whether tokens seen or compute were matched across models, so the data-scale effect is confounded with composition. No uncertainty is reported for the zero-shot trends. This study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship to parameter count, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fits or extrapolations to larger runs are tested.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal trend is tested.
The study does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study tests protein-model downstream performance as pretraining data grows, not power laws in held-out loss. It does not test image/video modalities, repeated-data training, or fine-tuning scaling.
It tests downstream protein-fitness prediction against pretraining-data snapshots, but not a broad relationship to pretraining loss or scaling in parameters or compute.
It does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices. Data composition and task strata are examined, but not as fitting-method sensitivity.

rows.subject: AMPLIFY embeddings with ridge regression
rows.stage_stated: pretrained embeddings with supervised ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream prediction across pretraining years and labeled-data amounts using random train/test splits.

conditions.value: Random; train/test ratios from 10/90 to 90/10, each replicated five times with different random seeds

rows.measure: Spearman correlation with experimental DMS scores
rows.value: There are minimal performance differences across AMPLIFY models; one-hot encoding outperforms model embeddings until a large volume of labeled data is used. Ridge-regression correlation is 0.52 when training on 10% of the dataset and around 0.675 when training on 80%.
rows.note: The stated numerical values describe the effect of labeled-data amount; the result relevant to pretraining scale is the reported minimal difference across AMPLIFY models.
rows.check: The numbers in the value (0.52 at 10%, ~0.675 at 80%) measure labeled-data amount, not pretraining scale. Only 'minimal performance differences across AMPLIFY models' bears on V6.

rows.note: The result separates the effect of labeled training groups from the absence of a consistent pretraining-year trend.

relationships.condition: ProteinGym zero-shot average across yearly snapshots
relationships.reason: Performance is non-monotonic, with a stated consistent drop from 2018 to 2021 despite about a billion added sequences (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Zero-shot performance declined consistently from 2018 to 2021 despite about a billion additional sequences.

relationships.reason: Low Neff/L proteins generally get worse with later snapshots (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Proteins with low Neff/L generally performed worse with later pretraining snapshots.

relationships.condition: Medium/high-MSA-depth and Organismal Fitness proteins, zero-shot
relationships.reason: These strata generally or steadily improve with later snapshots; the medium and high strata do so only partially (R4, R5, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Later snapshots generally improved Organismal Fitness predictions, with only partial improvements in medium- and high-MSA-depth groups.

relationships.condition: Stability, Activity, Expression and Binding assays, zero-shot
relationships.reason: These categories show fluctuating or flat trajectories rather than steady gains (R7).
relationships.display_finding: Stability, Activity, Expression and Binding performance followed fluctuating or flat trajectories rather than steady gains.

relationships.condition: Supervised ridge regression on pretrained embeddings (random, contiguous and modulo splits; β-Lactamase one-dataset transfer)
relationships.reason: There are minimal differences or no consistent trend across pretraining years; β-Lactamase stays at ~0.6 across all models (R8, R9, R10, R12).
relationships.display_finding: Supervised results showed minimal differences or no consistent trend across pretraining years, with β-Lactamase performance staying near 0.6 across models.

relationships.reason: Correlation improves from ~0.25 to >0.6 with later snapshots on all four datasets, though no power law is fitted (R11).
relationships.display_finding: Prediction correlation increased from approximately 0.25 to above 0.6 across all four datasets with later snapshots, without a fitted power law.
